questions.prompt: A burst of notification jobs overwhelms a downstream service. What does a buffering queue primarily provide?

choices.text: Automatic synchronous completion before enqueue returns.
A guarantee that every job completes with no latency.
Decoupling of job arrivals from processing rate.
Unlimited downstream capacity without changing the service.

questions.explanation: The queue smooths demand and separates producer timing. It does not create infinite capacity or eliminate processing delay.

sources.title: Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern
sources.claim: A queue buffers variable arrival rates and lets a service process work at its own pace rather than eliminating sustained capacity limits.

questions.prompt: Several workers consume one queue using competing consumers. How is this different from publish-subscribe fan-out?

choices.text: The producer must pick a fixed worker for every message.
Each message is assigned to one consumer for a processing attempt.
Every worker must receive each message as a broadcast.
Workers can process only one global message at a time.

questions.explanation: Competing consumers share work; publish-subscribe delivers to each subscriber. Work need not bind to a fixed instance.

sources.title: Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern
sources.claim: Multiple consumers distribute independent work, but consumer throughput must respect downstream capacity and differs from broadcast publish-subscribe.

sources.title: Competing Consumers pattern
sources.claim: Multiple consumers distribute independent work, but consumer throughput must respect downstream capacity and differs from broadcast publish-subscribe.

questions.prompt: A worker commits a change and crashes before acknowledging the message. What must the handler tolerate?

choices.text: The same message may be delivered again.
The broker automatically rolls back every external side effect.
The producer must create a different operation for the retry.
At-least-once delivery guarantees no duplicate processing.

questions.explanation: The message can be retried even though an external side effect succeeded. Idempotent handling protects against repeating that effect.

sources.title: Competing Consumers pattern
sources.claim: Competing-consumer queues can deliver messages more than once after failures; operations should tolerate duplicate processing.

questions.prompt: One malformed job fails on every delivery and keeps returning to the queue. Which response fits the pattern?

choices.text: Retry it indefinitely with no delivery limit.
Assume another identical worker necessarily repairs its content.
Delete every healthy queued job to preserve order.
Move it to a dead-letter path for analysis.

questions.explanation: Poison-message isolation prevents endless failure cycles and retains evidence. Adding identical consumers does not fix malformed content.

sources.title: Competing Consumers pattern
sources.claim: Competing consumers do not guarantee global ordering; repeatedly failing messages should be isolated rather than retried indefinitely.

questions.prompt: Arrivals remain faster than consumption for several hours. What should the design expect?

choices.text: Every message is automatically completed when storage fills.
Buffering guarantees a constant zero-age backlog at any rate.
A growing backlog unless capacity or input rate changes.
The queue eventually processes messages without any consumers.

questions.explanation: A sustained rate mismatch accumulates work. Queues separate timing but do not manufacture processing capacity.

sources.title: Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern
sources.claim: Queuing smooths intermittent peaks but does not remove downstream processing limits.

questions.prompt: Doubling workers increases database contention and slows all jobs. What is the useful next decision?

choices.text: Raise the worker limit without measuring downstream throughput or contention.
Tune consumer concurrency around the database bottleneck.
Keep doubling workers because queuing guarantees linear speedup.
Broadcast each message to every worker to reduce duplicate work.

questions.explanation: The bottleneck constrains throughput. More concurrency can worsen contention; broadcasting repeats work and does not solve capacity.

sources.title: Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern
sources.claim: Consumer concurrency can overload a dependency and should be matched to downstream capacity.

sources.title: Competing Consumers pattern

questions.prompt: Which load-leveling statements hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A queue gives each message zero waiting time during a large burst.
A queue can buffer intermittent demand peaks.
Producers and consumers can operate asynchronously.
Adding a queue eliminates every sustained throughput bottleneck.
A queued response means downstream processing has already completed.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: Buffering often introduces waiting time. B is correct: The service can consume work at a manageable rate. C is correct: Enqueueing and processing are decoupled. D is incorrect: Backlog still grows if arrivals exceed capacity for long enough. E is incorrect: Acceptance and completion are separate events.

sources.title: Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern
sources.claim: A queue buffers variable arrival rates and lets a service process work at its own pace rather than eliminating sustained capacity limits.

questions.prompt: Which consumer-scaling choices are appropriate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Add consumers for independent work when capacity permits.
Respect the capacity of dependencies used by the workers.
Monitor backlog when deciding whether consumer capacity is sufficient.
Assume increasing workers always helps a saturated database.
Require every worker to process every queued item to share load.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Parallel processing can increase throughput. B is correct: Excessive concurrency can overload the downstream service. C is correct: Queue depth can reveal pressure on processing. D is incorrect: More workers can increase contention at the bottleneck. E is incorrect: That is broadcast rather than competing consumption.

questions.prompt: Which duplicate-handling claims are sound? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Track processed messages when that is needed for deduplication.
Treat at-least-once delivery as an exactly-once side-effect guarantee.
Assume the queue reverses a database commit when acknowledgement fails.
Acknowledge every message before doing work to guarantee recovery.
Design processing so repeated delivery does not repeat an unintended effect.

questions.explanation: A is correct: A stored identity can identify an already applied operation. B is incorrect: Delivery can repeat after failure. C is incorrect: The queue does not automatically undo an external transaction. D is incorrect: Early acknowledgement can lose work if processing then fails. E is correct: Idempotent operations tolerate retries.

sources.title: Competing Consumers pattern
sources.claim: Competing-consumer queues can deliver messages more than once after failures; operations should tolerate duplicate processing.

questions.prompt: Which ordering and failure considerations matter? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Capture repeatedly failing messages for investigation.
Retry a poison message forever as the only error policy.
Assume all parallel consumers finish messages in creation order.
Do not assume competing consumers preserve global processing order.
Use supported ordering mechanisms when the workload requires them.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Dead-letter handling isolates poison work. B is incorrect: Unbounded retries can consume resources indefinitely. C is incorrect: Variable work duration can reorder completion. D is correct: Concurrent consumption can change ordering. E is correct: Some brokers offer sessions or similar grouping.
